title: Yunus Emre
hookLine: the Turkish folk poet of divine love
tomorrow: can you complain to God and still be faithful?

lines: A SLAMMED DOOR, THEN A PRAYER.
A BROKEN HEART, A PRAYER THAT ISN'T.
WHERE DOES LOVE OF GOD SHOW?
cards: It's possible to snap at your brother, slam a door, and ten minutes later stand up to pray as if nothing happened. Yunus Emre, a Turkish folk poet, has an answer to that, and it isn't soft.
In one poem he says: if you've broken a heart even once, the prayer you're praying isn't prayer. All the peoples of the world together couldn't wash that off your hands and face.
So the question for today: where does the love of God actually show?

teach.b: Yunus answers in plain Turkish, the language of the people around him, sung in villages and lodges, not in learned Arabic. His poems are about love, 'ishq, for God, and they keep pointing at one place: the heart.
The heart is God's throne, he sings; God looks into the heart. So to break someone's heart is to knock over a throne.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said something close in Sahih Muslim: God doesn't look at your bodies or your looks, he looks at your hearts.
Yunus isn't telling anyone to stop praying; in Islam the prayer stays due. He's warning that prayer can't cover for a heart you've wrecked. Here's a neighbor who asks the same question.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."

Shared ground: worship of God can't skip over the person you've hurt. And one honest difference. For Christians, those are the words of Jesus, scripture, with a clear order: repair first, then the altar.
Yunus is a poet, loved but not scripture, and he gives no steps, only a warning that lands like a bell.
Two traditions, each in its own words.

how: In Turkey and beyond, Yunus Emre's poems are sung as hymns (ilahis) at Sufi gatherings and taught in schools; Muslims who love them keep the daily prayers and try to mend what they've broken between people.

games.q: you blew up at a friend this morning. now it's time to pray. what fits Yunus's warning?
o: pray as usual; the prayer itself wipes the fight clean.
skip the prayer until you've fixed things with her.
pray, and don't let it stand in for mending her heart.
games.why: the prayer stays due in Islam. Yunus's point: it can't cover a heart you broke. that still needs mending.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose heart you may have bruised lately, even a little. Write them a short text, a few plain, true words, nothing clever. Keep it as a version or send it later; for now, just let the words be honest.

wordCard.voice: Yunus Emre: the Turkish folk poet of divine love, who sang that the heart is God's throne, and that a broken heart empties a prayer.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: 'ishq, passionate love; in Yunus's Turkish it becomes aşk, love for God.

carryVoice: Walk out with this: love's plain words, because a heart is a throne. Poets, four of six.

sources.ref: Yunus Emre, Divan: 'Bir kez gönül yıktın ise / bu kıldığın namaz değil' (a broken heart empties the prayer) and 'Gönül Çalab'ın tahtı' (the heart is God's throne)
Sahih Muslim 2564 (God does not look at your bodies or forms but at your hearts)
